subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FEDERAL ASSISTANCE IN MOVEMENT OF ANIMALS AND FODDER

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FEDERAL ASSISTANCE IN MOVEMENT OF ANIMALS AND FODDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make an announcement with regard to dominion government assistance in the movement of fodder into the drought areas of Manitoba and Saskatchewan and the movement of livestock out of these areas.
Some three to four weeks ago the situation in these drought areas looked extremely serious, and it appeared at that time that very large quantities of feed would have to be moved in and a very large liquidation of livestock would have to take place. Fortunately, during the past two to three weeks widespread rains have greatly improved the feed situation. However, it appears that a considerable movement of both fodder and livestock will still be necessary.
The government has decided to participate in emergency programs to aid farmers and ranchers hard hit by drought on the prairies. One-half of the freight assistance now being offered by Manitoba and Saskatchewan will be paid by this government, and the policy will be effective as of July 1, 1958. Both provincial governments have undertaken to help farmers in the stricken areas in the shipment of haying equipment, fodder and livestock.
Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway will reduce by one-third existing freight rates on hay and straw moved
into drought areas and on livestock moved out of these areas up to a maximum of $10 a ton, from August 1 to April 1 next year. I wish to express my appreciation to the railways for agreeing to participate in these drought relief measures. The western provinces will negotiate with trucking companies for rate reductions similar to those agreed to by the railways.
Hay shortage in affected areas in Saskatchewan is estimated at 100,000 tons and in Manitoba at 15,000 tons. There is some surplus hay in certain northern areas of both provinces and in Alberta. It is hoped that this will be sufficient to meet the needs, but it may be necessary to import some hay from adjacent parts of the United States.
The Saskatchewan relief program went into effect June 16 and the Manitoba program followed on June 23. Both provinces are paying full railway freight for the round trip when equipment is moved to where hay is harvested. When trucks are used, 50 cents per mile is paid one way only. In Manitoba a 25-mile limit is stipulated and in Saskatchewan the limit is 30 miles. On homeward movement of fodder, provided the distance is more than 25 miles, Manitoba is granting 5 cents per ton mile up to $8 per ton. If fodder is moved by rail, two-thirds of the freight is paid to a maximum of $10 per ton. The railways, of course, will be absorbing the other one-third.
In Saskatchewan 5 cents per ton mile is paid on harvested fodder moved by truck provided the one-way distance is 30 miles or more and up to a maximum of $7.50 per ton. Half the railway freight on harvested and purchased fodder is paid to a maximum of $10 per ton. However, there is a Saskatchewan stipulation that 4 cents per ton mile will be paid on hay that has been purchased provided the one-way distance is 30 miles and up to a maximum of $7.50 per ton.
In both provinces, when livestock is moved out of the drought areas for pasture or winter feeding, freight assistance is granted. Manitoba pays 2 cents per head per mile on the one-way distance for cattle and horses over one year old, and 1 cent per head per mile for cattle and horses under one year and sheep of all ages. Saskatchewan grants 2 cents per mile per head on the one-way distance for cattle over one year and 1 cent for cattle under one year.

Fear of heavy liquidation of breeding stock with resultant losses to owners and long-term damage to agriculture in the drought areas, together with some general depression in livestock market prices, prompted the decision on federal aid.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Starr (Minister of Labour) moved
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-42, to

provide for the resumption of the British Columbia coast steamship service operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to bring about a settlement by agreement of the differences between the parties to this dispute which has, of course, a long history.
We have been directly interested and concerned in this matter, as I told the house yesterday, since July of 1957, but its origins date back considerably beyond that time. The question is now being brought before parliament in this way because of very special circumstances not usually present in a normal impasse between labour and management. Among other circumstances are, of course, the extreme hardship to which a substantial number of Canadians who are in no way parties to the dispute are being subjected by the failure to reach agreement between the company and a part of its employees. It might be well at this point to emphasize that over half the employees of the company have signed a two-year agreement providing for an 8 per cent increase in pay. It is the difference between the company and the remainder of its employees which creates the present situation.
The hardship imposed on those who are not directly involved is very real. It is not merely a matter of inconvenience or discomfort to them; in many cases the livelihood and welfare of both individuals and communities are threatened. As a matter of fact, it is not too much to say that for many it involves serious problems in their supply lines for the necessities of life.
In this situation the government is faced with two alternatives. We can either do nothing, allow the strike to take its course and at the same time allow these communities to suffer, or we can take positive action to bring home to both parties the seriousness of the situation and provide new procedures under the authority of parliament which will supply a new initiative and, perhaps, a new climate in which settlement by agreement may be reached.
The bill provides, in the interim, for the immediate resumption of this essential service by the appointment of an administrator with the necessary powers. In effect the bill ends the strike so far as its impact on innocent bystanders is concerned, but it provides for the resumption of negotiations between the parties vitally concerned within the existing rights of each. To this extent it may be said to reactivate the normal procedures of collective bargaining which have broken down after 12 months of almost continuous settlement attempts.
Canadian Pacific Steamships
Yesterday I gave the house a resume of these attempts and indicated the many steps which have been taken by the Department of Labour to bring the parties together through the good offices, first of the conciliation officer, then of a board of conciliation, then of an industrial commission of inquiry and, finally, of the minister himself, in personal intervention and direct talks with the principals of both parties.
The situation has been further complicated by a dispute which tied up the only alternative water communication between the mainland and a number of island communities. That is now before the courts, and I will say no more in this connection except that the uncertainty of this situation is one of the factors which was taken into account before a decision to introduce this bill was reached.
In addition to appointing an administrator and providing for the renegotiation of differences, this bill also makes provision for the establishment of an additional procedure in the event that the dislocation of vital communications and the resulting hardship to large numbers of people develops into emergency proportions. I do not predict, Mr. Speaker, that this will happen. The government will use every resource at its command to prevent it from happening. But should it happen the consequences would, in our opinion, be tragic if all we could say to those who were suffering was that our hands were tied and that there was nothing we could do about it, whether because parliament was not in session or for some other reason. That would be the position if this bill were not to have the assent of parliament, because-and I wish to emphasize this-we have already availed ourselves, and so have the parties to the dispute, of every statutory provision now existing for reaching a settlement.
The bill, therefore, provides that the parties themselves, if they wish, may refer any matter on which they are unable to agree for decision by an independent board. It will also be possible, as a last resort, for the governor in council to refer any matter to the board under emergency conditions. The board would be empowered to act within the limitations of the revision or amendment of the existing collective agreement, either at the request of the parties or by the decision of the governor in council.
The bill also provides that the governor in council may make regulations to give effect to the decision of the arbitrator. The bill includes provisions to safeguard the right of employees who may have gone on strike to return to work without fear of being discharged from their employment because of

Canadian Pacific Steamships the strike action. It provides for the immediate withdrawal of the notice of strike, which will become invalid when this bill becomes law.
Many members of the house represent areas which because of their geographical situation could not be as vitally affected by a strike of this kind as the residents of the British Columbia communities in question. I need hardly say that many of the problems which face us as Canadians are geographic, and this is particularly so in matters involving vital communications. It is for this reason, of course, that the question of the proper limitations and responsibilities affecting government intervention very often arise in the communications field.
In the case of British Columbia on the one hand and our eastern maritime provinces on the other, the disruption of water communication over an uncertain and extended period can have widespread and serious results. In moving the second reading of this bill, I think I may properly request the sympathetic consideration by all members of this special aspect of the problem which underlies the bill before the house.
In conclusion, it may be well to explain to the house that there is an immediate provisional 8 per cent increase in the rate of wages. This will have the effect of providing a wage increase for the group of employees who will now go back to work, in line with the increase granted to the majority of their fellow employees, under the two-year contract effective June 1 of this year. This in no way prejudices the position of either party in the negotiations which will now continue.
I should advise the house that I will be asking one of my colleagues to move an amendment at the appropriate stage to provide that instead of a reference at the request of the parties or otherwise to a single person, the reference will be to a board of three, and this amendment will be made to clause 7.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposiiion):
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill which is before the house, and it is certainly a bill of an unusual character, is based on a resolution which was introduced in this house yesterday afternoon. Because of the urgent consideration which was requested, quite rightly, that resolution was passed through all its stages in this house in a couple of hours. The bill was then printed overnight, placed in the hands of hon. members this morning at about ten o'clock, and we are debating second reading of the bill at 3.15 this afternoon. Surely, therefore, there can be no suggestion that the opposition is holding up this bill or showing any other consideration than that of awareness of the urgency of the problem.

Nevertheless, we have our responsibilities to discharge in connection with this bill, and we intend to do that. Incidentally, when I say the bill was in the hands of hon. members at ten o'clock this morning I should add in fairness that it was in my hands in mimeographed form last night at approximately seven o'clock. I appreciate that courtesy, which I assume was also extended to the leader of the C.C.F. party.
The chronology of this unhappy business of a labour dispute which began, as the Minister of Labour has just reminded us, over a year ago and of a strike which began on May 16, is a monument to an inept governmental performance of which British Columbia has been the victim. As we see it-and there is a great deal of evidence to support the view and I hope to produce some of it-this procedure has exhibited a careless unawareness of a labour problem which was permitted to develop into a crisis, and which has created loss, distress, great inconvenience and business dislocation to an important section of the Canadian people. In the words of the minister himself it has caused "extreme hardship", and it has caused that extreme hardship not for days but for a good many weeks.
The question then that faces us in this house is this. Does the public interest which must be paramount now, require the end of this strike by legislative action of the kind suggested, with a renewal-and this is certainly indispensable-of the process of collective bargaining in some form?
Certainly the situation, as I have said, has been serious in British Columbia for a good many weeks now. I have read, and the information is no doubt founded in fact, that the strike has already resulted in the loss of $2 million to the tourist industry alone on Vancouver island, and that 30,000 tourist reservations in that island have been cancelled this summer. I suppose it is too late now to restore the position of the island in that regard.
I submit that an energetic and determined effort to solve this problem, not days ago but weeks ago, would in all probability have prevented what the minister has called this extreme hardship. Certainly it is true, as he has suggested, that Vancouver island has been effectively cut off from the mainland so far as Canadian water transportation is concerned or, as perhaps the people in Vancouver island might prefer to put it, the mainland has been cut off from Vancouver island. That is a situation, of course, that somehow must be ended even at this late date; and I take it this bill is designed-but as we see it not well designed-for that purpose.

We submit that if the right kind of action had been taken earlier it likely would not have been necessary to produce this kind of bill or indeed any bill. It would not have been necessary to rush it through parliament in a few hours after the bill was printed, without sufficient opportunity to study it and to consider whether amendments could be drafted to make it a better bill for the purpose in mind.
I have been informed that one hon. member of this house, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, in a telephone radio statement last night has criticized the opposition for obstruction and holding up this bill, for delay, when the bill was in the boxes of hon. members at ten o'clock this morning and we are debating second reading at 3:15 this afternoon. I do not think anybody is likely to be very much impressed by that kind of argument.
We are now faced with the situation that has been created, and we agree that in view of that situation water communication between the mainland and the island as a public service-because it is a public service, however it may be conducted-must be restored. We will not, therefore, oppose the bill, but we will certainly condemn the government for allowing a situation to develop which makes this bill necessary because of urgent practical considerations which makes this kind of hasty emergency legislative action necessary, the kind of action that should only be required of this house in times of great national emergency. Perhaps when we reach the committee stage we will be able to submit some changes in the light of the discussions that have taken place which will improve the bill. We will have to consider that as the discussion proceeds.
Let us look at the situation, Mr. Speaker. This strike, as I said, began on May 16 and is now in its 69th day. The seafarers' international union, a union which has more than once in recent years been the centre of controversy, representing 303 employees of British Columbia coast steamships, called its members off their jobs following the failure to reach an agreement with the company. The principal issue of course was, and remains one, of wages. As the Minister of Labour pointed out to the house yesterday afternoon, and he mentioned it again this afternoon, negotiations began with this union in the summer of 1957 and the existing contract expired, I think, on September 15, 1957.
No progress was made during those negotiations between the company and the union and on July 29 of last year, at the request of the union, the Department of Labour, as the minister has pointed out, appointed a conciliator
Canadian Pacific Steamships who met with the parties to the dispute I believe on five occasions. The conciliator reported on August 30, 1957, to the Minister of Labour that he had failed in his efforts to bring about an agreement; therefore a conciliation board was appointed at that time by the minister.
That board began its hearings on October 28 last. It filed its report with the minister on February 11 of this year. As the minister knows, three members of the board agreed unanimously on the recommendations covering 13 items in dispute, and the chairman of the board and the representative of the employer agreed on recommendations, I think, covering 10 other items in dispute; but in the matter of wages, which was the most important matter before the board, each member made a separate recommendation. The minister was good enough to put on Hansard yesterday what those recommendations were.
The chairman recommended a two-year contract; that wages be increased as of Sep-temper 15, 1958 by 16 per cent in the first year and 9 per cent in the second year, or a total increase over the term of the contract of 25 per cent. The employer representative -and this is interesting in the light of what is happening now and what is provided for by this legislation-recommended an increase of 12 per cent in the first year and if the agreement was to extend into the second year, a second increase in that year of 8 per cent, I believe.

speechtext: Five per cent.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
Five per cent, or a total of 17 per cent. The employee representative recommended something that I think would have given in terms of percentage about a 31 per cent increase over the period of the contract. Well, these recommendations of the board were rejected, and following that rejection the government on May 27 of this year appointed a commissioner of inquiry, Mr. Eric Taylor, who failed to bring about a settlement.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, May 27 of this year was the time when the government should have stepped in, or just after May 27, when the commissioner of inquiry reported that he had been unable to bring about an agreement; but that did not happen. The commissioner was asked to go back and try again. He failed and recommended voluntary arbitration, a recommendation which I understand was accepted by everybody but the seafarers' international union. There is a strike not only of this union but also of members of the association of marine engineers and the merchant service guild, and I shall do no more than just mention that fact.

Canadian Pacific Steamships
Now, Mr. Speaker, for over six weeks in this house the opposition asked a good many questions of the government as to what they were going to do both to recognize the seriousness of this situation and what they were going to do about it. I have those questions before me. Incidentally, there was only a single Conservative member in this house from British Columbia who asked a question on this subject during this period, and that question was asked by the hon. member for Victoria last May.
Why, Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned in the house yesterday, we were told as late as Tuesday of this week by the Minister of Labour-after the Canadian Press had indicated that legislation was going to be introduced-merely that the government was giving serious consideration to the matter. That was said in answer to some questions asked by the hon. member for Laurier. Why, nine days ago on July 15, according to the press, the Prime Minister wrote to the president of the associated members of commerce of Vancouver island to the effect that the government was restricting its efforts to mediation. Presumably at that late date there was no suggestion to the parties in dispute that legislation might have to be introduced by the government.
We did not take very much time yesterday in discussing the resolution, but we did take enough time to try to find out whether the parties to this dispute had in fact been informed in advance that in default of agreement there would have to be legislation. Surely, Mr. Speaker, this is a very important matter. It has a very important bearing on the possibility of settling this dispute without legislative interference. When we asked this question yesterday the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 2578 of Hansard:
I think it was made very clear that unless some amicable agreement was arrived at it would be necessary for the parliament of Canada to act.
Shortly afterward, on the same page of Hansard, the Minister of Labour said the government had not given any intimation during the discussion that any such action would be taken. But having said that, he went right on in the same intervention to say, and I quote from page 2579 of Hansard:
-but we did point out that if the parties did not arrive at a solution themselves action would have to be taken.
Well, that statement in its two parts seems to me to be contradictory and therefore somewhat confusing. That statement was supplemented by the minister a minute or two later, when he said:
This particular action was discussed last night in all aspects with one of the parties interested.

By "last night" I presume he meant Tuesday night. Naturally we queried him about this, and he amended that answer as follows, as reported on the same page of Hansard:
We explored every avenue and had discussions with both parties about the possibilities of legislation at this time.
Well, I am quite sure that leaves the house in a state of confusion, doubt and uncertainty about this very important aspect of the problem. Surely, therefore, Mr. Speaker, we have the right to know when the parties to this dispute were told that legislative action might be necessary. In what terms were they given that information, namely that if they did not come to an agreement themselves parliament would be asked to act? Because I can imagine no more important incentive to get the two parties to agree than to tell them that if they did not agree, tell them in specific terms at the earliest stage possible, last May, if you like, that if they did not come to terms parliament might be asked by the government to act.
The conclusion that we on this side of the house have come to is that the government did not act energetically and effectively to meet this situation and did not show an appreciation of the seriousness of developments. I think it is quite unwarranted to say, then, that everything had been done that could have been done.
The Vancouver Sun said on June 5, and I quote from that paper, that the present situation-
-was brought about, in part, by the federal government's failure to find a means of settling the C.P.R. strike. These vessels, unlike those of Black Ball, are under federal regulation. Ottawa seemed apathetic so long as the Black Ball line was open for business. It appeared that Ottawa was content to play for time.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that that was not the time to be playing for time. On July 17, three weeks or so later, the same newspaper had this to say:
The federal government persists in treating British Columbians-and Vancouver island residents in particular-as second class Canadians.
For two solid months now it has neglected or refused to take decisive action to bring an end to the strike tying up the Canadian Pacific's Princess fleet.
In the same editorial we find the following:
The Canadians living in these two parts of British Columbia certainly deserve as much consideration as Canadians living elsewhere. So far they aren't getting it.
Why, Mr. Speaker, earlier in May, immediately after the strike started, the mayor of Victoria and many others on Vancouver island and in British Columbia generally did their very best to impress on the government the seriousness of the developing situation.

The mayor of Victoria is reported by the Vancouver Sun as saying in May that acting under the authority of an emergency meeting of business and civic leaders he had tried to reach the Prime Minister or transport minister Hees by telephone for a whole day, and that he was unsuccessful. He wired the Prime Minister, according to this newspaper report, asking a telephone call at the Prime Minister's convenience, but he had not received one and he added, "I am disappointed and very concerned that the people of this area are being ignored." That was last May.
On June 11, of course, it is true that the Minister of Justice was in British Columbia after the failure, I take it, of the federal mediator, Mr. Taylor, to find an acceptable solution to the dispute. The minister is reported as having said at that time that attempts would be made at another level to reach agreement, and that the matter would be put before the labour department in Ottawa. The matter had been before the labour department at that time for a good many months, and that kind of response does not seem to me to indicate an awareness of what was happening.

I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this somewhat easygoing procedure is in startling contrast to that followed by the previous government in connection with the railway strike in 1950. Some hon. members will remember that the strike began on August 22 and that parliament acted on August 30 to end it, eight days later. That was only 12 days after the mediator appointed by the government on that occasion had announced that he had failed in his task. In other words, 12 days after the mediator appointed by the government to end the strike announced that he had failed, the strike had been ended by parliamentary action.
Notwithstanding the speed and efficiency, as I believe, with which the government of that day acted, which was due in large part, as hon. members who were here will remember, to the vigorous personal intervention of the prime minister of that day to bring the strike to an end, what did the opposition then say about the steps that were taken? The present Prime Minister, who was then a member of the opposition, had this to say as found on pages 73 and 74 of Hansard for August 30, 1950:
Urgency there has been for months. While the urgency of the situation required action by this
Canadian Pacific Steamships government and while our economic position in this country was worsening week by week, the government was vacationing.
And again:
-for days . . . the government did nothing. The government was not giving that leadership which the people of Canada had a right to expect.
The present Prime Minister castigated the government of that day for not taking action sooner than one week after the strike had been called.

speechtext: The trouble had been going on for months.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR

The trouble had been going on and action was being taken by the government. A strike took place. A special session of parliament was called, and within a week of the strike being called the strike was over. What are we then to say about a government which has been unable to take effective action in connection with a transport strike which has been going on since May 16?
As a result of this inability to bring the strike to an end in any other way, we now have a bill before us, a bill which as I understand it-some of my colleagues will have more to say about its details later-seems to me to be unclear in spots, which perhaps may create as many problems as it solves, and certainly warrants a great many questions being asked about it. Parliament is now being asked to intervene by passing legislation compelling strikers to go to work. That is a very unusual role for parliament and one that no member of parliament enjoys. However, that is what we are being requested to approve at this time. The first question that comes to mind, of course, is what principle is the government acting under in submitting this legislation? The Prime Minister had this to say yesterday on this point, as found on page 2578 of Hansard:
-it would be necessary for the parliament of Canada to act; that public security and maintenance of a proper regard for the rights of others would demand the introduction of such legislation.
Presumably that is the principle he had in mind in asking the parliament of Canada to act. I can see all sorts of possibilities of danger in the adoption and extension of that principle, "a proper regard for the rights of others", as justifying parliamentary action in a labour dispute. The Minister of Justice also had something to say on this point. As found on page 2582 of Hansard, he said with respect to the question of the principles under which the government was acting:
Of course, Mr. Speaker, the government recognizes that it is a matter of concern to the government on behalf of the people of Canada to see that the people of Canada are served with adequate transportation facilities, and I suppose that is the broad general principle involved in the bill.

Canadian Pacific Steamships
Then he went on:
We-
The government.
-felt the interests of the company required it.

We felt the interests of the country required it; we know we have the legislative jurisdiction to do it, and we propose to submit this proposition to parliament for its approval if parliament agrees with the course being adopted.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, orders strikers back to work by section 4. That, of course, is an unusual and very significant provision in a legislative enactment, and one which is bound to arouse a good deal of questioning in every member's mind. Every member of the house wants to be absolutely certain that he understands what is meant by this and that he has some appreciation of the government's position in justifying it, because the clause now reads that every employee who is now on strike shall return to the duties of his employment. It includes everybody, every employee who is now on strike.
This is not a situation such as existed in 1950 in the railway strike, when the strike had only lasted for a few days and the employees were available and ready to go back to work if a settlement could be reached.	This strike has been going on
since May 16, and now legislation is being passed ordering every employee on strike to go back, every employee who presumably was working on May 16, which is quite a long time ago. What about those employees who may have left the province during these weeks? What about employees who may be, if you like, out of British Columbia and in Nova Scotia? Are they to be ordered to go back and resume employment as it was on May 16, with the changes submitted in the legislation?
What about the situation that has been created by the Canadian Pacific disposing of two ships? Must the men who worked on those ships, and who are no longer in the employ of the company, be given work; or

must they, under this legislation, be compelled to go back to work on ships which are now no longer part of the company's fleet?
Yesterday when we were discussing the resolution the hon. member for Laurier asked this question, which appears at page 2580 of Hansard:
What is the position with respect to the other members of the other union, that is the S.I.U.? Do they go back at an increased wage?
The Minister of Labour is reported in Hansard as replying:
I cannot say with certainty that they would go back, but I expect and have every hope that they will-
I hope we will hear something from the government side as to the exact meaning of this compulsory back to work order. What happens to men who were employees of this company last May and who now either desire not to go back to work or are not in a position to go back to work?

I shall do my best to keep my remarks within the ordinary application of the rules on second reading, and restrict them to questions of principle. There is, of course, an important principle involved in clause 6 of this bill. The principle is that collective bargaining is to be resumed, and nothing could be more important than that in a bill of this kind. However, Mr. Speaker, this principle is not subject to any time limitation, and the proceedings could go on indefinitely. Yet there is no incentive, indeed there is quite the reverse, to reach an agreement within the terms of this legislation by the ordinary processes of collective bargaining.
For instance, the men are going back to work with an increase in wages of 8 per cent, which is considerably less than that offered to them by the employer's representative on the board. Surely that is not a proposal which is going to commend itself to the men, when it is less than they would have obtained from the employer representative's recommendation. Nor is it going to be an incentive to the company to make an agreement with the men, when the administrator is operating for the company on the basis of an 8 per cent increase. Aware of this difficulty, and aware of the possible complications raised by the fact that nothing in this bill puts a time limit on the negotiations and bargaining at the end of which perhaps the matter might again have to be looked at by the government, we asked the Prime Minister yesterday, if there was no agreement what happens then?
The Prime Minister said, as reported on page 2579:
On this occasion-
He was contrasting the procedure with that of 1950.
-we simply make provision to get the men back to work and the ships in operation. ... If other eventualities arise, and I am not here for the purpose of trying to envisage what the possibilities might be, then in that case, of course, we will be placed in a position where, if other action is necessary, it may be taken at that time.

Perhaps that was one of the reasons why the compulsory arbitration provision of that legislation was not required. We do not know what will happen under this legislation. We do know that there is not going to be a very great incentive to the company to bring about an agreement with the union when the members of the union are being paid an increase less than the employer's representative recommended.

I meant that in connection
with the railway settlement under that legislation, agreement was reached and the compulsory arbitration provisions of the legislation were not required and were not used. I am suggesting that in this legislation there is provision for compulsory arbitration in this clause, because the governor in council has the power to take action to that end if the government feels it is necessary. But it is an indefinite provision, and there is no time limit. There is, of course, no certainty that it will ever be used, or that that kind of action might be taken. I suggest, however, there are great possibilities of confusion and danger in that kind of indefinite, unlimited power being given to the governor in council.
There are other provisions in this legislation with which we will be able to deal when we are in committee. But quite apart from the particular issue of the strike and the desirability or necessity of getting this service resumed, I suggest we should take advantage of this situation to bring this whole matter very forcibly to the attention of the House of Commons so that we as a parliament may give consideration to a new policy for communication between Vancouver island and the mainland under modern conditions, and perhaps prevent this kind of

Canadian Pacific Steamships situation developing again in the future. Surely it is obvious to all, in the light of what has happened, that the island now must have adequate all year round secure water connection with the mainland.
The question is not, as I understand it, whether or not it is profitable. That matter is important, just as it is important when a new six-lane highway that is considered to be essential has to be built. But while the question of profit is important the question of service is even more important, and indeed is a paramount consideration with regard to this matter. It would therefore perhaps be well at this time for the government, if it saw fit, to initiate immediately a federal-provincial survey by experts to examine and report on the most efficient and least costly method for a combined highway and short-haul service between the island and the mainland which might even be considered if you like, as part of the trans-Canada highway system.
There is also, Mr. Speaker, the even more important, indeed the fundamental question of federal policy and federal responsibility with regard to the settlement of industrial disputes of this kind in the light of changing conditions. As early as 1950, in connection with the railway dispute of that year to which I have already referred, the present Prime Minister made a strong plea for a parliamentary committee to re-examine and restate the principles of collective bargaining. He will remember his plea; it can be found in Hansard 1950 at page 74. Again on January 9, 1957 he advocated-and I quote from the Hansard of that day-as follows-
-a revision of the conciliation methods and procedures in the interests of flexibility and the prompt settlement of industrial disputes.
He also advocated, and I quote further- -improvement and modernization of the machinery for conciliations.
Perhaps this situation in British Columbia has driven home to us all the necessity for doing something along those lines. On March 9, 1958, during the election campaign the Prime Minister is quoted by the Vancouver Province as stating in that city that his party wanted legislation to prevent long delays in settling industrial disputes.
I suggest to the Prime Minister and the government that this is a good time to carry out or begin to carry out that promise. That kind of action may help the government in avoiding in the future the kind of deplorable situation which has developed over this strike; and certainly, Mr. Speaker, it should save the people of British Columbia and of other parts of Canada from the unhappy consequences in the future of a situation such as that with which we are faced 

today, when the intervention of this parliament is required to settle an industrial dispute.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to deal with the second reading of this bill I should like to say first that I certainly associate myself with the general remarks of the Leader of the Opposition as they apply to the great delay that has taken place in dealing with this question. I may not agree with some of the other things the hon. gentleman said but with his approach, from the general point of view that there has been unnecessary delay, I agree.
I think first we should probably look at the conciliation machinery under the Department of Labour at the present time and attempt to determine why it has failed to operate in this case-because it resulted in a strike some weeks ago-and why it has generally failed to be of much benefit to labour-management relations over the years. In attempting to look at it in that light we might find part of the reason why this government found itself in a quandary as to what to do with respect to the situation on the west coast of British Columbia.
We have had the same machinery in effect for some number of years now and have used it in the same manner without any attempt on the part of the government-and I am not confining my remarks to this particular government; I refer to the governments that were in office during the period of time this legislation has been operative and up to now -to appear to grasp changing psychological forces that were at work in labour-management relations. This criticism is not confined to the federal field either; it applies equally well to all the provincial governmental conciliation proceedings that I know of. Ever since the end of the war there has been a failure to realize that changes are taking place, that there are different attitudes on the part of management and on the part of the unions also, and that there is a different industrial picture now from that which existed some years ago. Nevertheless the legislation and the philosophy of the people administering it have not kept pace with those changing times. That is probably one of the major reasons why we find this particular situation at the moment.
Certainly the closing remarks of the Leader of the Opposition with respect to an overhauling of the legislation and an overhauling of the machinery were most pertinent. That is something that is certainly long overdue. If this government will undertake to realize that fact and attempt to deal with the matter, perhaps in the future we shall have the type of legislation and the type of attitude on the

part of the people administering it that will be conducive to the settlement to differences of opinion between employees and employers when matters get to this stage.
While the government spokesmen have indicated from time to time over the past few weeks that they had this matter under consideration, I would submit that the only reason they finally took action to deal with it was that the government was forced into it. They were forced into taking action from the point of view, as the Leader of the Opposition pointed out, of the Black Ball ferry service being discontinued as of last week, the result being the cutting off of all shipping services between the mainland and Vancouver island. In addition I would submit also that the government was forced into action by a number of Conservative backbenchers who apparently have been under considerable pressure from their constituents to get some action on this particular strike.
We all know that probably every part of the province of British Columbia has a willingness and a desire to see the service reinstituted and to see a settlement of this dispute. We all know, especially those of us who come from British Columbia and who have travelled on these steamship lines between the island of Vancouver and the mainland on many occasions, the detrimental effect the strike has had on people living on Vancouver island, especially during this tourist season. We here in the House of Commons, in considering this bill, must look at it having in mind the great responsibility we have to the general public and for the economic welfare of the area affected by the strike.
It is true that the bill has only been in the hands of hon. members for a short period of time. It will, I think, require fairly lengthy discussion, and we will have to analyse main principles and some of the subsidiary principles involved before proceeding to an examination of the various clauses. We must look at the bill in the light of discharging our responsibility to the general public, and if an extended discussion does arise I hope the house will not consider that those who ask questions or make comments are doing so merely to delay the proceedings, but that they are merely seeking to understand the bill and its implications adequately before consent is given to its passage.
In this regard, while I did not see the news report to the effect that the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor) had, over radio or television or in a telephone interview, last night deplored the fact that the opposition was delaying the passage of this bill, I think that if he did so-and I do not know whether he did or not-he owes an apology to members of the opposition
Canadian Pacific Steamships parties, especially since he knows that the bill was not in our hands this morning until twenty minutes or fifteen minutes to ten o'clock. Certainly, last night there could have been no possibility of delaying the progress of this legislation.
I think it may be well to explain in a little detail some of the events which took place during the negotiations leading up to the cessation of this service, because I am sure that not only those who are directly affected by this service, or lack of service, but all members of the house would wish the employees of this company to be amply rewarded for the work they perform. It may be that a review of some of the wage rates and some of the changes that have taken place over the years would be of interest to the house and the country in considering this matter.
According to information compiled by the British Columbia federation of labour and the Vancouver labour council, the average wage rate paid to the seamen, to the employees, on these runs at the time of the strike, was from $1.31 to $1.35 an hour, which may be compared with the minimum wage in a number of other industries in British Columbia of $1.60, $1.70 and $1.75 an hour.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: What about their perquisites, the perquisites they get in connection with their employment, such as free meals and free board.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
I was talking about wage rates. Free meals and other things are in addition to that, but I mentioned wage rates because both the minister and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) indicated today that this question was the main problem at the root of this strike, not board and lodging. That is all I am talking about. The only increase these men have had since 1953 has been in the neighbourhood of $19 a month and, averaged over a 40-hour week-it would work out less if averaged over a week longer than 40 hours-it means an increase of approximately 10 cents an hour since 1953.
The junior chamber of commerce of Victoria had an interest in this matter, and I am sure the hon. member who asked a question just now may be familiar with the investigation which was carried out by that organization. In an attempt to provide a public service, in accordance with one of the objects for which it was formed, the junior chamber of commerce interviewed representatives of the C.P.R., representatives of the union, and Mr. Taylor who was the commissioner appointed to consider the dispute, and posed a number of questions to the individuals concerned.
2614	HOUSE OF
Canadian Pacific Steamships I am not going to read this three-page document in toto, but if any hon. member would like to see it he would be welcome. Chamber of commerce representatives posed some questions to a Mr. Frame of the C.P.R. on the wage structure and its relation to the fare structure, and so on. Four or five very important questions were put to Mr. Fraine in an attempt to discover, for instance, what a certain wage increase would mean with respect to a fare increase; the comparison between the transportation rates of the C.P.R. and those of other companies; the effect of special fare structures during particular seasons of the year; and so on. To all these important questions Mr. Fraine's answer, generally, was: "I do not know", or "We are not too sure on this point." The conclusion reached by the junior chamber of commerce, was that the union has considerable merit in its demand for increased wages. This, the conclusion added, would appear to be supported by the fact that the company's nominee and the chairman of the conciliation board respectively advocated increases of 17 per cent and 25 per cent. The report added:
We feel the onus is upon the company to take the lead in view of the fact that the union has dropped from its original exorbitant demands to a figure similar to that recommended by the chairman of the conciliation board and further because the company's nominee recommended a figure approximately the mean of the company's present offer and the union's current demand.
The question of whether or not either of the parties, or both of them, have up to now been bargaining in good faith is one that need not be referred to at this time and, probably, one person's interpretation with regard to this will be just as valid as another's.
In our efforts to discharge our responsibility to the public who are suffering hardship because of this strike we must be careful not to destroy any of the fundamental rights of either of the parties in dispute. I do not think we should attempt to interfere with what we have developed in Canada, with what is considered as the free play of forces between industry and management in labour negotiations. I doubt very much whether we are not, by considering the passage of this bill, or some parts of it, laying the ground for the destruction of some of these fundamental relationships between union and management. Questions such as penalties have to be considered, but that we can deal with later on in the bill.
Apart from the principle enunciated yesterday and today that this bill represents an attempt to get the line back into operation, there is another principle set out in the bill. In this regard the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) was questioned yesterday about what would happen if the bill passed and


if, after the parties sat down to negotiate, they failed to reach agreement. What steps would be necessary following upon that? I believe the Prime Minister misled the house or did not give us a complete account of what was likely to happen when he made his answer. I quote his remarks as recorded at page 2579 of yesterday's Hansard. I believe the Leader of the Opposition quoted these remarks, too, although for a different purpose. The Prime Minister said:
In 1950, of course, provision was made for compulsory arbitration under the legislation, and we opposed that at that time. On this occasion we simply make provision to get the men back to work and the ships in operation.
I take from the remarks of the Prime Minister yesterday that he and the members of his party were opposed to compulsory arbitration in 1950. Surely they should be consistent and oppose it now. Although he said this bill would simply make provision to get the men back to work and the ships in operation we find there is another purpose to this bill which lays the groundwork for the cabinet or the governor in council to institute compulsory arbitration in this particular instance.
We in the C.C.F. have not changed our position in this respect since 1950 and I can appreciate why the Leader of the Opposition did not make reference to this. Our position with respect to compulsory arbitration is the same as that we held prior to the election in March and prior to the election last June. Of course on close examination of the bill we note that it provides for compulsory arbitration and we can see, therefore, that the opinions of other parties in the house in this respect have changed. The establishment of the principle of compulsory arbitration is just another indication of how little real thought the Conservative party gave to the statements it made when its members sat on this side of the house. They merely sit and listen to the parties argue and say, "well, we will make some sort of report and we hope it is accepted." We find people being appointed as conciliation board chairmen who in some instances have no conception or no understanding at all of labour-management relations and have no intention or no desire to solve a dispute or to attempt to solve it. They merely say, here, I am a retired banker, or something of that sort, and here is an opportunity for me to rake in some government money, I will take the appointment but I will not do anything drastic to solve the dispute. I hope the parties solve it among themselves; if they do not, it is too bad. That is the unfortunate attitude that has developed over the past few years.
This government, Mr. Speaker, and the Liberal government before it, are equally guilty in failing to grasp the circumstances arising out of changing times and in failing to grasp the changed attitude of both parties to an industrial dispute, the changed psychological approach they have, and the government has failed to adjust the legislation accordingly. So long as we have the present legislation on the statute books which is outmoded and has relatively little effect, we are going to continue to get in these sorts of difficulties. We have to bring our legislation up to date. I hope this is one political promise which the Tories made which they will live up to, namely revamping our legislation.

Mr. Speaker, this bill as I read it this morning contains four principles upon which the government intends to proceed in order to dispose of the dispute. One of these principles is the appointment of an administrator who shall act as the agent of the company for the purpose of controlling and carrying on the business of the company. Another is that forthwith upon his appointment the administrator shall resume the carrying on of the business of the company which was suspended because of the


strike and that every employee of the company is directed by this legislation to return to work. Another of the principles laid down in the bill is that there shall be an increase of eight per cent over and above the amounts contained in the collective agreement which existed prior to the enactment of this legislation. Finally, as soon as the ships have been put into operation the steamship company and the union shall enter into negotiations with a view to a settlement of the matters in dispute under the authority of the administrator.
I should like to say that while the opposition will support the legislation because of the urgency of the situation and also because of the special circumstances involved in the dispute, nevertheless it should be pointed out to the government that there are a number of inherent defects and weaknesses in the legislation. I should like to couple my remarks with those of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) in his reference to the delay that occurred prior to the introduction of the legislation. Yesterday in answer to a question the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) gave reasons indicating that there had been no delay and proceeded to put on Hansard in chronological order the actions taken by the Department of Labour. While it is true that the normal processes of the Department of Labour were available during a large part of the duration of the dispute, still the position remains that the government should have indicated much earlier that this legislation was necessary. I am somewhat surprised at the statement the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) made earlier today that the government found itself faced with two alternatives. One of those alternatives was to do nothing and allow the strike to carry on, the other alternative was to proceed by way of legislation as it is doing now.
I say to the Minister of Labour, and to those associated with him on the other side of the house, that if they had proceeded in this manner with reference to another strike, namely that of Canadian National Steamships, perhaps they would have succeeded in saving those eight ships of the crown corporation. Instead of doing this, however, they did absolutely nothing in connection with that dispute. They did exactly what the Minister of Labour says was represented by one of the alternatives before him in the present circumstances, they did nothing and allowed these steamships to be transferred to the flag of one of the West Indian countries. They even went so far as to allow a number of the crew from the West Indies to be flown to Canada. It is true that in the middle of the flight instructions were given to have the crew returned to the West Indies.

I do not want to transgress the rules of this house by laying too great stress upon the dispute of Canadian National Steamships, other than to say this. The circumstances were not entirely different. It is true that, having regard to the stoppage of steamship service on the west coast, this dispute was much more serious than the other. Nonetheless, many of the circumstances which we find here were found with reference to Canadian National Steamships, and in that case I repeat the government took no action, whereas if it had acted as it has in this case, then that service would have been saved.

Therefore, I intend to support this bill in principle, but I will make a suggestion -one that is not new; it has been made by others-that the measure be changed in one respect at least to remove the part that deals with compulsory arbitration.
I feel, after studying the bill and reading it several times, that the desired results can be achieved without that part in section 7 which deals with compulsory arbitration. Under the terms of this bill-and I think I understand the situation-if the industry and its employees cannot get together and hundreds of thousands continue to suffer hardship, the only group which can move is parliament, and parliament is being asked to move -and it is very unwilling to do so, I think- and through parliamentary action we provide that the service has got to be resumed. Right. I imagine they will obey the law.
After resumption the owners of the industry and the representatives of the workers will get together and try to settle their differences. There is no time limit. As I interpret the act the government will maintain their administrator there until there is agreement between the employer and the employees, whether it takes a day or a year. Then you do not need that vicious principle which so many of us oppose, the introduction of compulsory arbitration.

I could be wrong, but I do not think I am, in saying that the C.P.R. does not want the government running its business. It wants to operate its own C.P.R. line and I believe it will do everything it can to get its business back into its hands. I consider this will be their approach. Equally, the employees will not want to continue working with only an 8 per cent increase in wages. They will want to work out something which will approach more closely their original demands, or what they were offered in varying degrees by various people. From the point of view, of the employees, then, it will be desirable to reach an agreement with the company. It may be asked: why have they not done so in the past? The answer is that they were not able to do it. The company had the power of lockout, and the employees had the power of strike and, as a result, agreement was not reached.
But now, with the action which the government has recommended, and with the service being resumed, there is no basis on which the two parties can proceed except that of trying to get together and negotiate a settlement. So, from a logical analysis, I say they are going to work out an agreement and because of that I sincerely recommend to the government that they remove from this bill a provision which is not required and one which is hated by almost everybody in this country, that is compulsion. I ask the government to remove something which is certainly hated by the trade union movements, namely compulsory arbitration. I am convinced that the entire intent of the bill can be met even with the removal of that clause and I commend that thought to the government.
I am going to conclude with just a little repetition and say that it would be extremely easy to wax wrathful about this type of legislation, to condemn one side and commend another, but I am not going to do that. I believe that as we ask industry to have a sense of responsibility and as we ask trade unions to have a sense of responsibility, then I must accept responsibility also when I stand in my place in the House of Commons and so I say, in these remarks, that much as I dislike the legislation I do not think the government could have done anything else in the circumstances and it will have my support.

Mr. Speaker, I am going to take the time of the house very briefly indeed. I may say with about the same reluctance and for some of the same reasons I take the same view as was taken by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) about being willing to support this legislation. I represent a province which is largely an island


and though it has almost twice the population of Vancouver island-I might point this out to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) -still, there are over 250,000 Canadian citizens on Vancouver island who have been deprived of a service which has existed for a very long time and which is, in my view, an essential national service. We know that the service to Newfoundland and to Prince Edward Island, the other two large inhabited islands on our shores, is guaranteed by the constitution and while the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) refuses to be drawn into any discussion about whether Canada has any obligation to maintain this service, it seems to me that by the fact the government has seen fit to introduce this extraordinary legislation it is admitting that.
I am very troubled not only about the feature of the bill that the hon. member for Vancouver East is troubled about but also about the failure of the government to enunciate any principle on which this action is taken. I think perhaps we can discern the principle. I have tried to suggest a principle that there is an obligation in the case of Vancouver island that perhaps does not exist in the case of Pelee island although we do subsidize a ferry to Pelee island, as I happen to know. In other words, this is such a large segment of the total Canadian population that it is a national problem. I am personally of the view that it is a national problem. It seems to me that by its failure to state any principle on which it is acting and by its failure even to state clearly, as the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) pointed out, on what section of the constitution it is basing its action, the government may be, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) suggested, letting itself in for an awful lot of trouble and pressures of all kinds in the future.
This is a precedent that none of us likes any more than any of us who were associated with it-and I was not in parliament at that time though I knew something of the circumstances-liked what was done in 1950. It is a very disagreeable thing for the parliament of Canada by law to oblige or compel people to work. Indeed, some of the bitterest struggles in the history of our country were over the question of whether or not we should compel people to fight when the very life of our country was at stake. Here we are picking out a small segment of our population and saying that these people have no right to choose where they shall work, that for an absolutely unlimited and undefined period of time-because there is no time limit in this legislation-the members of this union unless they die or become incapacitated-and I presume they would be

let out on those grounds-are going to be compelled by law to go on working for this company or for the administrator acting in some capacity in connection with this company.
It is difficult for me personally and I believe it is equally difficult for all hon. gentlemen on this side of the house to understand why all the workmen who went on strike on May 16 should be compelled to go to work whether they have moved to Newfoundland or Nova Scotia in the meantime -presumably as long as they are within Canadian jurisdiction-in view of the fact that there may be no work for them. There is no similar compulsion in the bill for the company to keep all the ships in operation.
In the Vancouver Sun of July 23, 1958 we read that two of the strike-bound ships have been sold. What are the crews of these ships going to do when they turn up in obedience to this law and find there are no jobs for them? There are obviously not going to be as many jobs as there were on May 16 as was pointed out by the hon. member for Laurier a few moments ago. Which employees will the government compel to go to work? How will the government choose which employees will be those who will be compelled to go back to work?
It seems to me this is one respect in which the legislation is not fair as between the employer and the employees. All the employees have to go back to work but apparently the C.P.R. does not have to put back in operation all its ships and we have heard rumours to the effect that two more ships may be sold. The government should insert a provision in this legislation by which the C.P.R. could not sell any more of its ships as long as this statute is on the statute books. There has been a lack of foresight and forethought here on the part of the government.
I am sorry that the hon. member for Vancouver East is no longer in the chamber.

I want very respectfully and with due regard to his very much greater experience in this field than mine-and I do sincerely respect the hon. gentleman's experience-to point out that under the conditions that will be created if we pass the bill in this form there can be no fair collective bargaining once this bill is in operation because the C.P.R. will have no incentive whatsoever to agree. It is going to be paying an 8 per cent wage increase. The union is asking for a lot more. Why should not the C.P.R. continue to pay the wage prescribed in this statute and never reach an agreement? There is no incentive on the side of the company whatever. If we do not have some way of
Canadian Pacific Steamships terminating this provision there is an indirect compulsion on the men far greater than any direct, clear and unequivocal compulsion stated by parliament in the law could possibly be and the legislation as now drafted is not fair as between the employees and the employer. It does not hold the balance fairly between them but creates a very strong bias on the side of the employer against the employees.
There is another thing about the legislation that troubles me very much and which I thought would have troubled the Minister of Justice, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and most of the hon. gentlemen who kept us here for over a month in the summer of 1955 debating the Defence Production Act because it gave certain extraordinary authority to the governor in council to be exercised in secret and with no time limit on it. The powers that Mr. Howe was asking for at that time did not include the power to compel human beings to work for an indefinite time at a fixed wage. That was one thing that was not included in the Defence Production Act. Here we are being asked to pass a statute without any time limit on it. If the Minister of Justice would like me to remind him of it, he will find on page 4733 and again on page 4737 of Hansard for June 13, 1955, his eloquent pleas for a time limit on that arbitrary legislation. I am not going to break the rules of the house by reading clause 7 but we are being asked in that clause to give the governor in council power to prescribe any kind of arbitration that he deems expedient.
When the government in 1950 brought in the maintenance of railway operations legislation, what did it do? It prescribed precisely what the arbitrator could do. It said, in the first place, that he could not reduce the wages under any circumstances. This bill does not say that. It said furthermore that he must begin his determination within 30 days, and that it was to be done according to prescriptions carefully laid down by parliament on behalf of the Canadian public whom we represent. Here we are being asked to give to the governor in council to exercise in secret -as hon. gentlemen opposite were so fond of saying, as the Prime Minister made most of his political reputation by saying-by order in council the powers, and they are asking that this arbitrator shall have the power to make any kind of arbitration, that some day when this parliament is not sitting, when we are away at our homes and the government gets into another panic, as they did over this strike after 68 days they will suddenly decide to ask the arbitrator to do something.
I do say that this is not good enough. I do think that the government should either do

Canadian Pacific Steamships what the hon. member for Vancouver East suggests, knock this provision out of the bill entirely-though I see grave difficulties about that because it means that these men are going for an absolutely indefinite period to be subject to this wage, to being compelled to work at this wage for an indefinite period- or else the government should put a time limit on that portion of it and parliament should be allowed to prescribe the conditions of the arbitration in great detail.
I would not object to the idea so much that perhaps the governor in council might decide to meet the point of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), that the governor in council might have the power to prescribe some longer period if the parties were getting together and were in the midst of negotiation, but it does seem to me we should not have timeless legislation of this character. That is the argument the hon. gentlemen put up.
As I say, the powers of the other legislation did not include-and I repeat this-the right to compel a small group of Canadians to go to work and to stay at work at a fixed wage for an absolutely indefinite period. This, it seems to me, is important and I go back to my first point. It is essential to restore this service. I am happy that all parties in the house are agreed on it; I am happy, particularly because I do represent an island, and I know how the people on an island feel about the isolation there can be if communications are interrupted. I have even experienced interruptions which are caused not by man but by nature and know something about how inconvenient and awkward they can be; but, at the same time, I do feel that to ask us to pass legislation that is to stay on the statute books indefinitely, that has no time limit of any kind upon it, as the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Laurier have pointed out, is to ask us to do something which hon. gentlemen opposite made the main point of their campaign in the session only three short years ago.
It seems to me there is another point-and this is the only other point I wish to make at this stage-which troubles me a good deal about this legislation, and this was also mentioned by the hon. member for Laurier. I am merely repeating perhaps to underline it. In the case of the maintenance of railways operations legislation in 1950, parliament was restoring the operation of the two great railway companies, one of which is owned by the taxpayers of Canada, and if it incurs any deficit that deficit has to be met by the parliament of Canada, anyway. The other at that time was quite clearly not losing money; therefore, there was no question that this legislation would be putting directly or indirectly any charge upon the taxpayers.
[Mr. Pickersgill.)
But it does seem to me that we are not at all clear as to what this legislation is doing to the exchequer. The minister should tell us that there should be some provision in the legislation itself which makes clear whether, if these ships are operated at a loss, that loss is to be borne by the Canadian Pacific railway or, if not, is it to be borne by the taxpayers of Canada and if so on what authority is the government going to pay that loss? This seems to me to be a very serious question. Are we being asked to say that the people of Canada, through their parliament, are taking away the private property of a company, operating it at a loss, if that happens, and then making the shareholders of that company pay that loss? That is a very new principle, a very new thing to be doing, if that is what we are doing. If we are not doing that, what are we doing? The legislation, it seems to me, does not give us any clue, any answer to that question.
If there should be a fortuitous profit, which I assume is very unlikely, but which might conceivably happen, what would be the situation? But that question is not nearly as serious as the first question. If there is a loss incurred in this operation, particularly if it is a greater loss than the Canadian Pacific railway has been experiencing-I believe they claim that they have not been operating those ships at a profit; we do not know much about it, at least I do not know anything about it- under what authority is parliament imposing that on the C.P.R. or on the taxpayer? Surely, it is one or the other, and we should not pass legislation that does not cover that contingency.
But I come back to what seems to me the most serious thing of all and what has been emphasized by my leader and by the hon. member for Laurier, and what I feel I must emphasize again. Here we are in this legislation engaging in a kind of compulsion, which I think is even worse than compulsory arbitration, namely compelling men to go to work at a fixed wage for an indefinite period. That is what we are doing. Let's face it. That is what the law says and they are subject to the penalties of the law. If they do not go back to work they are criminals, and we are not even saying that there is to be work for them when they get back because of the two ships being sold, if they have been sold. But what is most serious of all is that we are giving to the governor in council this power to provide for any kind of arbitration that the governor in council may see fit. We are being asked to do that. I do hope that the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice or the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) will rise in his place and tell us that some kind of

definite prescription will be put into section 7 of this legislation and that some kind of time limit will be put either on this provision that those people must work at this wage or that in some way or other there will be some definiteness about this matter.
Because it is an emergency, because we recognize that Vancouver island should not be cut off from the mainland, we do not feel that we should oppose the principle of what the government is trying to do any more than the hon. member for Vancouver East felt that he should, but we do oppose the indefinite character and the effect of this legislation. I know the government can say, just as we said with far better reason three years ago, that we would not do any of these things, we would not let that go on indefinitely. The hon. gentlemen will not forget, and certainly I will not, the debate we had at that time about that time limit, and that was only about the power to do things to things, not the power to do things to people. Here we are being asked to take action for an indefinite period, we are being asked to give the government, or the administrator appointed by the government, the power to compel men to work at a fixed wage with no guarantee of any kind that for all that period the wage will be changed regardless of changing conditions.
It seems to me that this is so grave a defect in this legislation that, while we are most anxious to co-operate with the government in getting this thing through as quickly as possible in order to end what I am ready to regard as a national emergency, we still think that they should do something about those points that I have raised and which, I may say, were raised previously by the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Laurier.

Because of the fact that we believe firmly in collective bargaining we have endeavoured to use every means we possibly could think of to bring about a solution to the situation through collective bargaining between the parties and through mediation and the facilities of our department.
May I say that in the appointment of the commissioner of inquiry every possible formula was exhausted by him that could be thought of and he spent four to five weeks doing this in conjunction with the parties to the dispute. During that period of time there was nothing else the government could do as long as the negotiations were in progress. However, the stage was reached where the commissioner of inquiry reported to the Minister of Labour that he had exhausted all efforts and he made certain recommendations. Therefore all in all throughout the whole negotiation of the dispute there has been no time lag whatsoever.
The hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) suggested that the bill should be referred to the standing committee. Under ordinary circumstances that might be the right procedure but at the present time, with the situation as critical as it is in this particular instance, I say that would certainly cause greater delay and greater hardship. The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) wanted to know who the administrator would be and whether we were prepared to announce his name. I feel that should not be done now when we are in the process of dealing with the bill but the name of the administrator will be announced after the passage of the bill by parliament.
The hon. member also referred to having a look at the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act to see whether the legislation could be brought more up to date in order to deal with present problems. I might say to him that one of the first actions I took on assuming office was to ask for advice and suggestions from labour, management, in fact all interested groups in the country, as to how the act could be amended and improved to bring about better conciliation procedure and better collective bargaining between management and labour.
