If the hon. gentleman would read the two extracts together, as I suggested they should be read, he would have the answer to his questions-that this is the maintenance of an essential service which the government of Canada recognizes as being a concern of government. It is on that basis we felt it was essential to act.
The hon. member for Laurier pursued in somewhat more detail the question of the constitutional validity of the legislation. He asked whether in view of the provisions of section 92 this matter came within the legislative competence of the parliament of Canada. I would answer him by saying it has been generally recognized over the years that this service is an essential part of the transportation system of the Canadian Pacific railway and that the transportation system of the Canadian Pacific railway is one which falls under federal legislative jurisdiction. And inasmuch as the service connecting the mainland of British Columbia with Vancouver island is an integral part of the Canadian Pacific railway's transportation system, it is therefore clearly within the exceptions contemplated by section 92, paragraph 10(a) and thereby comes under the general provisions of section 91, paragraph (29) of the British North America Act.
In addition, I would refer the hon. member to a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada as to the validity and applicability of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act recorded in the 1955 supreme court reports at page 524 in which the question of the jurisdiction of the dominion government in connection with labour disputes arising with respect to steamship companies of this sort was decided. The court had before it for consideration the applicability of section 53 of part II of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, and I am reading, now, from page 534 of the supreme court report:
53. Part I applies in respect of employees who are employed upon or in connection with the operation of any work, undertaking or business that is within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada including, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing,
(a) works, undertakings or businesses operated or carried on for or in connection with navigation and shipping, whether inland or maritime, including the operation of ships and transportation by ship anywhere in Canada.
The court found that the parliament of Canada had complete legislative jurisdiction in connection with navigation and shipping. The operations of the British Columbia coastal steamship service by the Canadian Pacific


Railway Company falls immediately and directly under that section of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. At that time Mr. Justice Kellock, as reported on page 561, found in part as follows:
In my opinion, therefore, such matters as wages, hours of labour, and agreements relating to conditions of labour upon ships, whether operated in local or interprovincial or international waters, are within the exclusive jurisdiction of parliament.
I may say that the court by a majority found that parliament had exclusive legislative jurisdiction in connection with labour matters on ships in Canada.

speechtext:
If the suggestion is that we cannot deal under section 1 with the question of penalties, which is a general matter arising out of other sections of the legislation, Mr. Chairman, it would seem to me that this would be the most appropriate place to deal with it; for, arising out of the discussion, it might be felt wise to make some revision in the bill or have additional clauses added or changes made in the present clauses respecting penalties. I would think that this would be the more appropriate place to deal with the question of penalties than section 4 or any other specific section. I should like to proceed along that line, if 1 may, Mr. Chairman.
The question of penalties is a rather important one, because certainly the bill sets out that there shall be certain things done and certain things shall not be done, or people should refrain from doing them. Specifically, every employee is supposed to return to his duties. The company is to refrain from discriminating against or discharging employees by reason of their having participated in the strike, and things of that nature. I would submit that the providing for penalties under the three relative sections of the Criminal Code which the minister mentioned is certainly not in keeping with our past practice or understanding with respect to penalties arising out of contraventions of the present Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, illegal strikes and things of that kind.
With my limited knowledge of the federal labour code or the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, I would point out that there is no provision in that act for jail terms being imposed on employees who contravene the act with respect to failing to work. I am thinking particularly of this. If this bill passes and a group of employees, in concert with one another, decide to refrain

from working, then they would be in contravention of the act and in all probability- this is a legal point-it would also be an illegal strike.
The other phase of it is that while the administrator is charged with the responsibility of carrying on the business of the company and assuring its continued operation, yet if the company likewise acted to prevent the employees from carrying on or working for it there would be in effect an illegal lockout. I would like to know what is the position of the company or of an employee or a group of employees who find themselves for one reason or another in an illegal strike or in an illegal lockout? Would they be subject to the penalties set out in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act which provides merely for fines in the case of an employer who declares or causes a lockout contrary to the act? He is liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding $250 for each day the lockout exists and every person who acts on his advice, and so on. Every trade union which declares or authorizes a strike is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine of $150 for each day, and every officer or representative of a trade union which authorizes or participates, and so on, is guilty of an offence, and again a fine is imposed.
It seems to me that we would be well advised to keep the question of penalties in line with the application of penalties for similar acts under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. I suggest that the providing of a penalty of a jail sentence, albeit the court may suspend it, up to a maximum of two years, is certainly not in keeping with the principle that we have adopted in contraventions of the present Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. I would appreciate it very much if we could have some clarification of that. In any event, I think we would be well advised to put a further section in the bill before us now restricting penalties for contraventions of it to the penalties which are set out in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I had better outline the general position under this bill and then deal specifically with the points raised by the hon. member for Skeena. Actually, several hon. members in the course of the debate on second reading asked the question, what happens to employees who are not now in the area and what happens, for instance, to employees who formerly were working on the two ships which were sold between the time of the commencement of
Canadian Pacific Steamships the strike and the present day? I would direct the committee's attention to the terms of section 4, which is the operative section here, which states, reading from line 12:
-every employee who is now on strike shall return to the duties of his employment-
So that an employee who is no longer an employee of the company, and who is not on strike but has left and taken other employment is obviously not covered, and not bound to come back to the work which he was doing on May 16, or before May 16, when the ships were still sailing. That is the first point that should be realized. The only ones who will be obliged to go back to their employment are those who now regard themselves as and are in the position of employees of the company and who are prevented from returning to work by the fact that there is a strike in force. Those are the only people to whom this legislation will apply.
Then, in the second place, the provisions of the Criminal Code, to which I referred earlier, will apply, in so far as employees are concerned, only to those who refuse to go back to work notwithstanding the provisions of this act. Once they have gone back to work, once the operations have been resumed and the men are working again then, as I understand it, with respect to the employees, the company, and the unions as bargaining agents, the penalty provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act will apply. It is only with respect to persons, if any, who defy the provisions of legislation enacted by parliament and refuse to go back to work, or refuse to resume operations, in the case of the company, or continue to counsel men not to work, in the case of a union, that the penalty provisions of the Criminal Code to which I have referred would apply.
Let us be quite frank about this. We do not contemplate, in fact we are confident that neither men nor unions nor company will defy legislation enacted by the parliament of Canada. It is for that reason, amongst others, that we have not put a special penalty provision in this legislation. The situation is, therefore, that we are satisfied that men, unions and company will co-operate to resume operations. Once that is done, then, as I have said, the provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act will apply. There will be a collective agreement in force by virtue of the legislation and if there should be any cessation of employment on the part of the men by strike action or lockout action by the company then, because there is a collective agreement in force the

Canadian Pacific Steamships provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act will apply.

Mr. Chairman, first of all
it was not my suggestion that a special provision should be put in the bill with respect to penalties but that the penalties applicable under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act should apply under this legislation. The question of employee-employer relations is involved, with which the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act also deals, and in my opinion to provide for penalties under section 107 and the other two relevant sections of the Criminal Code in the initial instance is to make special provision with respect to infractions of this legislation. In order to make things equitable across the board and to treat this dispute as we have treated all other industrial disputes or relations between employers and employees under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act in the past, I submit that the penalties under that act should apply and that we should not make the special provision of a two year jail sentence by way of penalty.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR

does not appreciate is that what we are doing here is enacting a statute to get the men back to work and to get the company to resume operations. It is only if there is defiance of the legislation that the penalty under the Criminal Code applies. I would ask my hon. friend whether he does not really agree, if there is concerted, deliberate defiance of a statute of parliament enacted to bring about the resumption of this operation that the penalty provided by the Criminal Code should apply, especially in light of the fact that once the operation is resumed, the ships are operating and the men are back at work then it is only the penalties provided by the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act that will apply. It seems to me that that is a reasonable situation to provide.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR

I understand the minister's interpretation of the application of penalties but I shall submit that the penalties should be set out in the bill and that they should not be as severe as those under section 107 of the Criminal Code in the initial instance involving an infraction related to not doing what the legislation provides in order to get operations resumed. The minister may have in his own mind a good understanding of the definition of "employee" and whether or not an employee is or is not on strike but I would submit that the interpretation he has given does not clear up the question. Some

years ago, when the O.B.U. and the industrial workers of the world were formed they attempted to establish the principle that when a group of employees went on strike it was not compatible with their theory of conducting strikes that any of the people on strike should go to work somewhere else. They attempted to establish the idea that if a person was on strike he was on strike and that was it. He walked up and down on the picket line and was not supposed to leave the picket line to try to earn income from some other source.
Since that time that attitude has changed. A number of unions now have strike funds and receive contributions from other unions with which they attempt to make relief payments to the people on strike. But they also promote the idea of as many employees as possible finding employment elsewhere during the period of the strike.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: Take another man's job away from him.

If the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) wants to participate in the debate in more than an interjectory fashion I suggest that he do so in a formal way by catching the eye of the chairman. I would also submit that his observations in this regard are probably no more accurate than those he made with respect to the efficiency of the employees working on these boats a few months ago. A person can be on strike and can be gainfully employed with some other company than the one against which he is on strike. Inasmuch as that situation now applies, is that person on strike or is he not? In his own mind he may say: "I am on strike against the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, B.C. coast steamships but I am working somewhere else in the meantime." Many people do it.
It is a question of the attitude of the individual whether he is or is not on strike and you cannot define the attitude of the individual in a statute. I submit that there will be a great deal of difficulty in attempting to apply the provisions of clause 4. I only deal with it because the minister raised the matter but I think it may be just as well to do so now. You will have a difficult time applying the provisions of clause 4 with respect to individual employees. Some employees may find work elsewhere and some who would like to work in some other occupation may not be able to. What is the difference between the two classes of employees? Unless we spell out the definition of "employee" more clearly there will be difficulty. It can be done under clause 2 or maybe under clause 4. I do not think that matters too much but we should spell out the

definition of "employee" more clearly so that it does not include individuals who consider in their own minds that they have left the employ of the company or individuals who, subsequent to the enactment of this legislation, decide that they no longer want to remain in the employ of the company. If you will spell that out clearly I think you will be in a much better position and will overcome the almost impossible task of legislating with respect to the feeling that an individual employee has when he is on strike and may be working elsewhere.

I should like to make one or two brief general observations, as I have not thus far participated in this debate. I agree, of course, with what the Leader of the Opposition has just said that in a matter of this importance, in order to preserve the freedom which is implicit in the principle of collective bargaining, there must be some limit, otherwise that freedom is not guaranteed.
Now, all of us in this house are confronted with a fait accompli presented by the administration. I must say, speaking for myself, I have had some difficulty with the position I took before six o'clock in registering my vote on this matter. I was 

influenced by the fact that the members in this house from British Columbia, particularly those who sit to my immediate right, thought that the statement of facts as presented by the government warranted their support. I do not know what is the situation in British Columbia. All I have is the statement made by the Minister of Labour, in whom I have great confidence, that the situation is one which, to use the ambiguous phrase of the Prime Minister, comes within the ambit of public security and the rights of others, but what I would prefer to regard in the light of the phrase used by the Minister of Justice, involves the public interest.
This situation is not unique. This kind of situation has arisen before within fairly recent times and the government did not bring forward the unusual legislation that is now before the house. When we were in power in 1955, I believe, there was a strike involving the Princess Helene which operates between Digby, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick. This situation resulted in a considerable amount of dissatisfaction and provided great inconvenience for the population of the area. No steps were taken such as those now proposed by the present administration.
But the government of the day has a responsibility and in the light of its responsibility it says to us "This is the situation; this particular procedure must be followed in the national interest". I think a member would be bold who disregarded the implications of that statement by the government. But as the Leader of the Opposition said this afternoon, it is one thing to be confronted with a particular situation and it is another thing to ask why that situation had to arise at all. My leader charged that the government had been dilatory in allowing this situation to eventuate; and because it has happened, we in this parliament are confronted with the necessity of taking the unusual step that is proposed. Was the government dilatory?

By the government as a whole, except through the Minister of Labour and more particularly through Mr. Taylor who was his commissioner in the matter. But compare this situation with the situation that confronted the government of Canada in 1950 when the prime minister of that day was, to the knowledge of every man in this house and of the country, engaged every minute for many days in continuous negotiations with both management and labour, so much so that when he announced the settlement of the strike the representatives of the union paid the then prime minister of this country a most unusual tribute when they referred to his ceaseless efforts, efforts which alone they said were responsible for the advantage which they had achieved. Compare that situation with the situation involved in this matter. The Prime Minister's only known participation was the announcement yesterday that the government proposed to bring forward or to carry out this unusual procedure. There was no indication of real effort being made day in and day out to avoid the necessity of coming to parliament and asking for unusual powers, powers which the present Prime Minister and others criticized with such great vigour in 1950. They said that freedom had been denied and that the lights of freedom had gone out as a result of the policies of the previous administration. As recorded at page 73 of Hansard of August 30 of that year the Prime Minister said:
That was and is our attitude. No one had objection to paragraphs 1 and 2, and to the noble preamble. What is being done in this section of the bill is what we take our objection to, namely the granting of uncontrolled and untrammelled power to one person to determine decisions in trade union matters and to change the provisions for settlement of labour disputes that have existed for over seventy years.

I believe that if the debates that have taken place on this bill lead to the setting up in parliament of a committee to re-examine and restate the

principles of collective bargaining, much good will result in labour relations. Evolution makes change necessary.
But let there be no mistake that what we are doing here is granting uncontrolled and untrammelled power to one person. This bill is a bill that gives untrammelled power to one person and it is introduced by a government headed by one right hon. gentleman who used this argument as a mighty weapon against the former administration. 1950. That is why the Leader of the Opposition has suggested there should be a limitation of time. Otherwise, the company would be put in a position of being able to exercise over the men a form of control that would negative any assertion that there existed the right of collective bargaining for the period of the contract under the control of the administrator to be appointed under section 7 of this act.
In addition, this particular measure not only provides for an unlimited period of operation but it provides that the men shall go back to work on conditions of income return which represent the lowest recommendation made by one member of the conciliation board. My hon. friend corrects me. It is lower than that. That was not the situation with regard to the bill of 1950. With regard to the bill of 1950 the men were given an economic advantage that would encourage them and encourage the company to arrive at an agreement through the processes of collective bargaining. This does not exist in these particular circumstances because of the fact that the men will receive eight per cent instead of, at least, the middle recommendation. They will operate in circumstances that are the least generous of any of the awards made by the members of the board of conciliation.
And so, as we deal with this unusual measure, reserving for ourselves each in the light of our own conscience what our attitude will be towards some of these clauses, let there be no mistake about it-this government which criticized the previous administration so much for the course that it took has placed itself, as a result of its own dilatoriness, in a position where it has had to take a course similar in principle.

speechtext: We have just seen the traps into which simulated indignation can lead exemplified in the speech of the hon. member for Essex East. The hon. gentleman is trapped coming and going and he is not even sure of the direction he is going in and he does not know what direction he would like us to go in either.
We are quite clear in our minds and intentions as to what we are doing, and we are clear that it is in the interests of the country and in the interest of the parties to the dispute. Let me remind hon. gentlemen opposite when they talk of the great courage they showed and the celerity with which they acted with regard to the railway strike of 1950, when they imposed compulsory arbitration with a time limit of one month, that there was another strike more comparable with the present one-a strike of the SS Princess Helene in the maritimes,-in which case they allowed the strike to go on for three months and did nothing.
Let hon. members opposite complain because we are doing something here tonight.
I was not quite sure, when I heard the hon. member for Essex East at the opening of his remarks, whether he was complaining because we had failed to act soon enough or because we had heeded and paid attention to the pleas of the people and to the pleas of hon. members from British Columbia. The committee will remember that he quoted with obvious relish a newspaper report about pressure being applied by what he called "rebellious British Columbia Tories". I am not surprised that he found that extraordinary, because there was never a Grit member on the backbenches, or a private member on that side who dared to rise in his place-

I see the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is back in the committee having avoided voting on the bill.
We are glad that we have members who make their views known in the house and outside the house and in the caucus and that our members dare to raise their voices in caucus. We do not have a C. D. Howe running our caucus, and certainly we have listened to the views of hon. members from British Columbia, as we have paid regard to the interest of the people of British Columbia. What we are doing here is quite clear; we are providing that there shall be a resumption of operations; that the company's
Canadian Pacific Steamships service shall be continued and that the men shall go back to work. Then we are providing for a principle in which we believe, and that is a resumption of negotiations looking to a settlement by the processes of free collective bargaining, and when hon. members opposite suggest we should be ashamed of having waited for 68 days, that is evidence of the difference between our party and their party when it was in power.
We believe in the processes of collective bargaining; they believe that governments should step in, and apply compulsion immediately, and they are trying to persuade us to do that. And then they believe that, having stepped in, governments should put a gun to the heads of the parties and say: you have a time limit within which to negotiate. Not only do they want to see in this bill the principle of compulsory arbitration, applied to the settlement of disputes, but they want a time bomb put in with the short limit of 30 days. That is what they did in 1950.
What they did in 1950 and what they want us to do today is to come to a situation in which the parties have negotiated for weeks and months and find themselves in fundamental disagreement, and then to say, "Now, you get back to work and negotiate and if you do not find a solution within 30 days then your negotiations are going to be blown sky high", so that violence will have been done to the principle of free collective bargaining.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: We do not operate in that way, Mr. Chairman. We have introduced a bill based on the principles I have outlined, namely that the people of British Columbia should continue to be served by getting these steamships back into operation, and that the parties should now be required to resume the process of negotiations without any time limit. Because we believe in the good faith of the Canadian people and we know that these parties are Canadians just as hon. members in this house tonight are Canadians, we believe they will recognize their responsibilities and accept that what the government did today was done of necessity after giving all the time that could be given up to now; and that with this bill in effect the parties will resume negotiations through the process of collective bargaining and will be able themselves to bring about a just and equitable settlement of the dispute.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have listened with a great deal of interest to my friend the hon. member for Essex East defending the action of the Liberal administration hither and yon with both barrels and condemning the government-although he probably did not mention it in those words-for introducing the question of imposed or compulsory arbitration. I have also listened to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice with equal relish attempting to decimate the Liberal forces and make reference to their attitude now and previously. It is one of the few occasions in my life when I find that I am in agreement with both hon. gentlemen.
However, I should point out that what these hon. gentlemen have been saying is incorrect for they both know-and my friend the hon. member for Essex East certainly should know-that the Maintenance of Railway Operation Act that was passed in 1950


contained words that definitely placed it in the category of legislation that imposes compulsory arbitration. He cannot get away from it no matter how he attempts to twist the words for in section 5 of that act the following provision appears:
-the governor in council shall appoint an arbitrator to decide all matters not then agreed upon between them that appear to the arbitrator necessary to be decided-
Whether or not the parties agreed to this was immaterial. The governor in council was to appoint an arbitrator if the parties failed to do certain things.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: That is not compulsion.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that is not compulsory arbitration but I submit that it clearly is the imposition of compulsion. That is the imposition of an arbitration board upon two parties to a dispute without their agreeing to it.
There are two ways in which you can obtain arbitration in labour disputes. One is for the two parties to agree to go to arbitration which has happened in the past and which, in fact, happens practically every day of the week in the interpretation of collective agreements and in the determination of whether or not a person was discharged for proper and just cause. In cases of that kind it has been mutually agreed between the parties that they should have arbitration. When arbitration is imposed on them from an outside source as it was in 1950 under the Maintenance of Railway Operation Act introduced by the former Liberal administration it is compulsory arbitration.
It is made compulsory, in the first place, that they participate in arbitration proceedings and the next logical step is that it is compulsory for them to accept what the arbitrator decides. It is the same principle as that enunciated in the bill before us, a principle with which hon. gentlemen opposite disagreed so strenuously when they were in opposition and concerning which they spoke in the last two election campaigns when they stomped up and down the country with their arms around the working class people saying, "You will never have this imposed on you in the future if you elect us".
This bill imposes compulsory arbitration because the matter must be referred to an arbitrator. I understand that subsequently this will be amended to read a board of arbitration but it is immaterial whether it is an individual arbitrator or a board because it is still compulsory arbitration. The principle outlined in this bill is that outlined in

the Maintenance of Railway Operation Act of 1950 and no matter how hon. gentlemen in the front benches of the Liberal party attempt to juggle the English language and no matter how hon. gentlemen in the treasury benches of the government attempt to twist the wording of this bill when referring to it, they cannot escape the fact that both parties have been guilty of introducing legislation that imposes compulsory arbitration upon parties to a dispute. This is the very principle that members of the government denounced in the last two elections and in years previous to them.
I have entered into a discussion of this matter only because it appeared that it was the intention on the part of both the supporters of the government and of the official opposition to say that this legislation and the act of 1950 to which I have referred are something that they are not. I think it would be well to put the question to the Minister of Labour point blank and ask if he agrees with compulsory arbitration or not.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to revert to the question of sanctions and the omission of any reference in the bill to sanctions or penalties which were mentioned by the hon. member for Skeena. There are at least five clauses in the bill which may provoke the imposition of sanctions of some kind either for any one refusing to return to work or submit to arbitration or for refusing to obey the directives of the administrator or in the event of disobedience to the provisions of clause 9 of the bill.
The Minister of Justice quite properly explained that sanctions or punishments are imposable under section 107 of the Criminal Code and he relies on that section for imposing punishments for disobedience or the violation of any sections of the proposed act.
I do not think it is the intention of the Minister of Justice or of the government to be as severe as the act allows in the imposition of punishments upon an employee who refuses to go back to work or who disobeys an order issued by the administrator because the punishment under section 107 of the Criminal Code is very severe, in my judgment. That section provides for the imposition of a penalty of two years imprisonment without the choice of another form of punishment.
The minister also referred to section 622 of the Criminal Code, which might provide for a money penalty in lieu of imprisonment. If he will read section 622 I think he will find that that is not a fact. Under that section you cannot impose a money penalty in lieu of imprisonment.
Section 107 of the Criminal Code, following the application of law, says very clearly, or
Canadian Pacific Steamships the judgments say, that the provisions of section 107 do not apply where the statute itself provides a penalty and a mode of punishment. The legislation now before us makes no reference to and provides for no mode of punishment whatsoever; consequently, in any penalty or punishment that was imposed we would have to fall back upon section 107 of the Criminal Code, and I do not think that that is the intention of the government.
I think the hon. member for Skeena did make a practical suggestion to remedy the situation. Perhaps the bill could be amended to say that in so far as a breach of any of the provisions of this legislation are concerned the punishment should be punishment similar to that which is contained in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, or some similar reference. I respectfully submit to the Minister of Justice that under good law, and in the application of the principle of law he should indicate in legislation of this kind the mode of punishment. If it does not say it directly, it should refer to some other statute which is similar in spirit and circumstances, and make the practice accordingly. I think that would certainly solve the question of the imposition of sanctions which I respectfully submit should be contained in the bill itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
I think I can only answer the hon. gentleman along the same lines as I answered the hon. member for Skeena, namely that this is not-if you like to call it that- a continuing statute which is liable to be the subject of continuing contravention in which you provide a scale of penalties. When enacted this will be a piece of legislation by which parliament directs a certain course to be followed in a certain set of circumstances. Therefore, it seems to me that the hon. gentleman himself, on reflection, would agree that where there is a wilful defiance of a statute enacted by parliament to deal with a specific set of circumstances the penalties made applicable by the Criminal Code should be allowed their normal operation. And, as I have pointed out, once there is a compliance with the direction of parliament-not of the government but of parliament-once there is compliance with that and there is a resumption of operation and return to work, then the penalties for infraction of this statute do not apply but the penalties provided by the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act will apply, because operations are in process and work is in progress and there has been compliance with this statute. Those penalties will, therefore, no longer be applicable.
I do point out, however, that section 107 creates a penalty for which there is a maximum sentence, not a minimum and, therefore, under the provisions of section 622, there is

Canadian Pacific Steamships the alternative of a fine and in both of those provisions it is in the discretion of the court, having regard to the nature of the offence, the state of mind of the accused and all the surrounding circumstances, to impose the appropriate penalty up to the maximum and only the maximum which is provided by the code.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: I respectfully disagree with the minister. I am simply observing that section 622 does not provide an alternative. It might provide an alternative where there is an additional form of punishment, an additional punishment to the imprisonment imposed. There is an alternative on the second level of punishment but not on the original.

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member is asking me a question based on a hypothesis. We have discussed these matters with the company and, as I said last night, I

have no knowledge of any present intention on the part of the company to sell their ships so the question does not arise.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it surely does in this way, that the company under the bill will have no right to control its business. That will be done by an administrator appointed by the government and subject to any instructions he may receive from the governor in council. Therefore if the company finds that it is operating this service at a great loss it has no control over its business and would not be able to take steps to reduce that loss by disposing of ships or in any other way without the approval of the administrator and, presumably, without the approval of the governor in council which gives instructions to the administrator. Therefore it is not the company now but the governor in council which will decide the operating policy of this shipping company under the administrator.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
I do not know whether I would go quite as far as to say that we will decide the operating policy of the company under the administrator. The intention is quite naturally that the day to day physical operation of the ships will be carried on by the company. There is no intention of putting in an administrator who will interfere and make radical changes with respect to the operation of the ships. He will not be qualified to do that. He will not have the staff to do it.
As to what would happen in the event of the eventualities arising to which the Leader of the Opposition has referred, I do not think it is possible or sensible for us to attempt to answer at this time because it will depend upon the circumstances in existence at that time. The purpose of the bill is to cause the resumption of operations and the hope and expectation is that the dispute will be settled within a reasonable time and a new collective agreement brought into force at which time, of course, the administrator will immediately be withdrawn.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION PROVIDING FOR APPOINTMENT OF ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is undoubtedly one of the most important features of the measure. The minister has said that the agent will be able to prevent the sale of the ships. He expanded on that in his answer to the Leader of the Opposition. Canadian Pacific Steamships agreement. That represents the lowest recommendation made by one member of the board.

What I find most objectionable is that we are being asked, and I admit I agreed to go along with it, to compel a group of men to go to work and remain at work at a fixed wage. That is what we are being asked to do and it is a pretty grave thing to be doing. That is what we are asked to do, yet the government will not tell us whether they might one day allow the Canadian Pacific to sell the ships out from under these men and leave them without jobs.
It does seems to me that this legislation is so extraordinary, and what parliament is being asked to do is so unusual-the kind of thing we want to do as rarely as possible- that the government should tell us they will not permit any of these ships to be sold for the duration of this act, or if they believe circumstances have arisen whereby, in the public interest, the ships should be sold, the government will report the proposed transaction to parliament before it is carried out. It does not seem to me that is an unreasonable proposition to make. The inference was left with us that the resumption of this service was in the national interest. If the resumption of this service is in the national interest, surely parliament is entitled to know what the service is going to be, how many ships there are going to be. Mr. Chairman, I have some comments to make about clause 7 (d). While the amendment proposed and adopted by the committee with respect to a board of three arbitrators was acceptable in terms of the numerical structure of the board of arbitrators nevertheless as far as we in this group are concerned one of the general provisions in clause 7 (d) is certainly not acceptable. I refer to the provision that empowers the governor in council to impose compulsory arbitration on the parties to the dispute when he may deem it expedient. There has been ample discussion about it and I do not think it necessary to repeat what has been said or to refer to attitudes that hon. gentlemen opposite had in years past which are not compatible with the attitudes they have at this particular moment.
I have an amendment to propose with respect to clause 7 (d) which I should perhaps explain first. The amendment provides for an arbitration board to consist of three as is the case with the present provision but it would also provide that the establishment of the board of arbitration would be done in the same manner as is the establishment of a board of conciliation under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. That is to say, each party to the dispute would select a member of the arbitration board. There would be a certain time limit-I believe of five days-during which these two appointees, one representing the union and one the company, would be able to decide whether they could mutually agree on the selection of a chairman of the board and if these two members could not so agree the Minister of Labour would appoint a chairman as is done in the case of a conciliation board at the present time.
The amendment would also provide that the arbitration board would have all the powers, functions and obligations of a conciliation board as stated in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. It has been the experience of those engaged in labour disputes that where agreement can be reached between the two disputants in the selection of a chairman of a board of conciliation there is less disagreement following the award of the board than is the case where the chairman of the board has been appointed by an outside party. It must be kept in mind, of course, that the decision of this board is an arbitrary one but nonetheless disagreements do arise over the awards of boards. The chairman is the key person and where agreement exists as to his selection there is less likelihood of difficulties arising following the award of the board of arbitration.
The provisions of the amendment would also provide that the arbitration board be


established only at the mutual request of the parties and that it not be imposed on them by the governor in council. Accordingly,
I move:
That clause (d) be deleted and the following substituted therefore:
For referring to a board of arbitration of three members to be constituted and appointed in the same manner as is a board of conciliation and investigation under the provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act and to have all the powers, functions and obligations of a board so constituted and appointed such matters relating to the revision or amendment of an existing collective agreement as the parties thereto may request, including the fixing of the term during which the new collective agreement shall operate and the day to which the agreement or any provision thereof may be retroactive, and for giving effect to any decision by the board of arbitration upon such a reference for the purpose of this act and the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, but no regulation made under this paragraph shall be deemed to limit or restrict the rights of parties to an existing collective agreement to agree to vary or amend any of the terms thereof and to give effect thereto.

Mr. Chairman, I think the position is that a union has signed a collective agreement with the company for an increase of eight per cent and that union is not coming under the terms of this statute. Therefore, their agreement is not subject to variation or subject to the statute in any way. However, the other three unions or organizations have no agreement with the company. We felt that it would not be proper to contemplate sending men back to work at different wage rates. If we put nothing in here, then the stewards' union would go back with an eight per cent increase and all the others would go back with no increase, so we felt that for the duration of the period while the statute is in operation and while they are back to work under the statute they should all be back with the eight per cent increase.
Therefore the three unions which have not signed new collective agreements go back under their old collective agreements which are provisionally amended by an increase of eight per cent. If, however, they and the management are not able to agree on an increase then it seems that the thing should go back to the status quo, namely, where it is now. If there is no agreement as to what should be the increase in wages and negotiations proceed on that basis under the statute and if negotiation fails and arbitration becomes necessary, arbitration proceeds on that basis. It did not seem proper to us to ask parliament here and now to legislate as to what should be the terms of agreement between the parties so that when negotiation commences and if arbitration should commence the thing will be free and open to arbitration and negotiation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

We felt that when they went back to work under the terms of this statute all the men who went back to work should go back to work at the same wage rates. The government should establish the basic floor of the old wage rate plus eight per cent below which a board of arbitration cannot go.
The government has no right to establish a board of arbitration which could grant by way of an award wage rates less favourable than their brother workers are getting under a collective agreement signed by their union of its own free will. All I am asking is that if a board of arbitration is imposed by the government that board should not be allowed to arbitrate below the present provisional rate. Whether such a board will or will not is another question as is whether or not the matter will ever get to that stage, but I submit that that protection should be given if parliament is to be asked to order people back to work, restore this service, appoint an administrator and particularly to give authority to the government to impose compulsory arbitration. Surely we have a right to ask for that little modicum of protection of the wage rates of the employees of the unions affected so that they will not go below the wage rates established by collective bargaining through another union.
